t: Check If a String Is a Valid Sequence from Root to Leaves Path in a Binary Tree
o: We must decide whether the array `arr` exactly matches some root-to-leaf path: node values along the path, read top-down, equal `arr` element by element, and the final node of that path must be a leaf (no children). In Example 1, `arr = [0,1,0,1]` matches the path 0→1→0→1 whose last node is a leaf, so the answer is true. In Example 2, no child with value 1 exists under the node 0 reached by prefix [0,0], so it fails. In Example 3, the path 0→1→1 exists but its last node has a left child, so it is not a leaf and the answer is false. Constraints are tiny (arr length ≤ 5000), so a single DFS/BFS traversal comparing values as we descend is more than sufficient — no clever data structures needed.
k: Match arr against a path greedily during one DFS — at depth i the current node's value must equal arr[i].
A match is valid only if the last matched node is a leaf; internal nodes matching the full array do not count.
Prune early: once a value mismatches or we run out of array before reaching a leaf, that branch dies.

a.i: Walk down the tree while consuming arr. At each node with index i, check the value equals arr[i]; recurse into children with i+1. A successful match requires i to be the last index AND the node to be a leaf. This naturally handles all cases including when the tree is deeper than the array.
s: Define dfs(node, i): returns whether arr[i:] forms a valid sequence from node.
If node is null or node.val != arr[i], return false.
If i == len(arr) - 1, return true iff node is a leaf (no left and no right child).
Otherwise return dfs(left, i+1) OR dfs(right, i+1).
a.t: O(min(n, m)) where n is the number of nodes and m = arr.length — each visited node does O(1) work and we never go deeper than m levels.
a.sp: O(h) recursion stack where h is tree height, bounded by min(n, m).

a.n: Approach 2: Iterative BFS with level tracking
a.i: Same logic as DFS but process nodes level by level using a queue of (node, index) pairs. Each dequeued pair represents a partial match of arr[0..index]. Push children only when their value matches the next array element. At the end, success means some pair reached index len(arr)-1 at a leaf. Useful if recursion depth is a concern.
s: Initialize queue with (root, 0); guard against empty root.
Pop (node, i). If node.val != arr[i], skip.
If i is the last index, return true iff node is a leaf.
Else enqueue matching children with index i+1.
If the queue empties without success, return false.
a.t: O(min(n, m)) — each tree node enters the queue at most once per matching prefix position, still linear overall.
a.sp: O(w) for the queue width w, up to O(n) in the worst case.

w: In an interview, lead with the recursive DFS — it is the cleanest expression of the idea and interviewers expect it. Mention BFS as an alternative if stack depth matters. Common pitfalls: forgetting the leaf requirement (Example 3 exists precisely to catch this), failing on a null root, and continuing to match after exhausting arr. Edge cases: arr of length 1 valid only if root itself is a leaf; a path longer than the tree height can never match. Follow-ups might ask to return all valid sequences, handle paths ending anywhere (not just leaves), or count matches — all solvable with small tweaks to the same DFS.
